meta.title: Who really said "Love all, trust a few, do wrong to none"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Yes — it's genuine Shakespeare. The Countess says it to her son Bertram in All's Well That Ends Well, Act 1, Scene 1 (First Folio, 1623).
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'Love all, trust a few, do wrong to none'?
meta.ogDescription: Genuine Shakespeare: the Countess's parting advice to Bertram in All's Well That Ends Well, Act 1, Scene 1 (First Folio, 1623).

answer.label: Written by
answer.sourceLine: Genuinely Shakespeare. The line is spoken by the Countess of Rousillon as she blesses her departing son Bertram in All’s Well That Ends Well, Act 1, Scene 1 — first printed in the 1623 First Folio. The exact wording is confirmed in the Folger edition ↗.

source.heading: The source

docMeta.dd: The Countess of Rousillon (to her son Bertram)

source.excerpt:
Be thou blest, Bertram, and succeed thy father
In manners, as in shape! thy blood and virtue
Contend for empire in thee, and thy goodness
Share with thy birthright! Love all, trust a few,
Do wrong to none: be able for thine enemy
Rather in power than use, and keep thy friend
Under thy own life’s key: be cheque’d for silence,
But never tax’d for speech.
trail: The exact lines appear in the Folger Shakespeare edition ↗ of Act 1, Scene 1.
The full parting speech is confirmed in the MIT (Moby) text ↗, spoken by the Countess of Rousillon.
Wikiquote ↗ lists the line in its sourced quotations for the play, Act I, Scene i.
source.excerptNote: The three famous clauses are the middle of a longer maxim the Countess gives Bertram; the popular short quote lifts them out of that speech.

source.rightsNote: All’s Well That Ends Well was written c. 1602–1605 and first printed in the 1623 First Folio — centuries before the 1931 U.S. copyright cutoff, so the text is firmly in the public domain.

author.name: William Shakespeare
author.heading: William Shakespeare
author.bio: William Shakespeare of Stratford-upon-Avon is the most-quoted writer in English, which also makes his name the internet’s single biggest magnet for invented “Shakespeare” quotes. This one, however, is real: it comes from All’s Well That Ends Well, one of his so-called “problem plays,” where the aphorism is put in the mouth of a character — the Countess of Rousillon — rather than spoken in Shakespeare’s own voice.

misattribution.heading: So what’s the catch?
misattribution.intro: The attribution to Shakespeare is correct — the only distortions are small ones of framing and punctuation.

items.who: A character, not Shakespeare speaking directly
items.why: The line is dialogue: the Countess of Rousillon says it to her son Bertram as he leaves for the French court (MIT text ↗). It’s genuine Shakespeare authorship, but it’s a mother’s parting advice inside a play, not a personal motto of the poet.

Popular versions render it “do wrong to none” with a lowercase ‘do’ and often a full stop. In the verse the clause runs across a line break — “Love all, trust a few, / Do wrong to none:” — and continues into a longer sentence, as shown in the Folger edition ↗.

misattribution.truthLine: Verdict: authentic Shakespeare. The words are the Countess’s parting counsel to Bertram in All’s Well That Ends Well, Act 1, Scene 1 (Wikiquote ↗).

context.heading: Why it resonates
lead: Stripped to three clauses, the line reads as a tidy rule for living: open your heart widely, extend trust narrowly, and injure no one. In the play it is more pointed — a mother arming her son with worldly caution as he steps into a court full of people who will not all wish him well.

The maxim doesn’t stop at those three clauses. The Countess goes on: be a match for your enemy in strength but slow to use it, keep your friend as close as your own life, and be blamed for staying quiet rather than for talking too much — a fuller, more guarded piece of advice than the greeting-card version suggests.
